It's not just the cost of materials. It's the availability of qualified workers. We need to really get behind training programs, training you know, ladies and men to get into the field. It's a great field. It's a great way to learn a living and it'll be here forever. So we need that. We need to work with our towns and all the towns will say they're behind it, but it's hard to get them to really do something, work on their zoning to make sure that zoning works so that we can provide the kind of housing that people need in each and every town. And I'm not talking just single family. I'm talking apartments and kind of Minions. And so there's all kinds of areas that need modifications, some changes to improve. These energy codes that are changing frequently can be both confusing not just to the builder but building inspectors. We need to have training behind that, but the cost associated with it. The objective can be good, but the cost associated with some or many of the changes really work counter to the objective of having a good quality affordable housing in our state and we need to work together to try to make sure that that's handled properly. So anything we can do to be helpful in that front, you know, each of these things have their own little nuances, as I said, so it really warrants a conversation to make sure that they're handled properly.
